speaker: Sholto Douglas
title: Is RL + LLMs enough for AGI? — Sholto Douglas & Trenton Bricken
question: In reinforcement learning post-training, what determines whether an AI lab builds detailed human-scaffolded curricula versus relying on sparse end-of-task rewards?
guest: It's an efficiency question. Obviously, if you could give a dense reward for every token—like if you had a supervised example—that's one of the best things you could have. But in many cases, it's very expensive to produce all of that scaffolded curriculum of everything to do. Having PhD math students grade students is something you can only afford for a select cadre of students, and you couldn't do that for all the language models in the world. So obviously that would be better, but you're optimizing this Pareto frontier of how much you're willing to spend on scaffolding versus how much you're willing to spend on pure compute. Because the other thing you can do is just keep letting the monkey hit the typewriter, and if you have a good enough end reward, eventually it will find its way. Different tasks sit at different points there, and a lot of it depends on how strong your prior over the correct things to do is. That's the equation you're optimizing: how much you're willing to burn in compute versus dollars on people's time to provide scaffolding or rewards.

points.core: Dense human-authored curricula become economically prohibitive to scale across every target skill.
points.note: Accept: high labor cost of expert-graded process supervision or bespoke human curricula limits scaling across all domains. Do not credit: claiming dense rewards are algorithmically inferior to sparse rewards.

points.core: Extra sampling compute can substitute for human scaffolding when end-task rewards are clean.
points.note: Accept: burning more RL rollout compute lets the policy eventually discover winning trajectories under a reliable outcome reward, forming a compute-versus-labor Pareto frontier. Do not credit: generic advice to use both data and compute.

points.core: Base model prior strength dictates where each task sits on the compute-scaffolding frontier.
points.note: Accept: tasks where the pretrained model already has a strong prior need less human scaffolding and can lean harder on sparse-reward compute. Do not credit: ignoring base-model capability or treating all tasks as having a single fixed optimal mix.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
The choice mostly comes down to whether the model can discover success often enough on its own for a sparse reward to carry a learning signal, weighed against the cost of building and maintaining the scaffolding.

If the base model already completes the task some non-trivial fraction of the time, an end-of-task reward (tests pass, answer verified, goal reached) is enough, and it scales cheaply. When tasks are long-horizon or far beyond current ability, successes are too rare, credit assignment across thousands of steps becomes noisy, and labs add structure: graded difficulty, intermediate checkpoints, rubrics, demonstrations, or shaped rewards.

Several other factors push the decision. Cheap, reliable automatic verification favours sparse rewards, whereas subjective outcomes need human-designed rubrics. Expensive rollouts make dense signals more valuable. Shaped rewards and curricula also invite reward hacking and bake in human assumptions about how to solve the task, so labs with strong models and ample compute tend to prefer outcome-only rewards, in line with the "bitter lesson". Finally, expert human time is scarce and doesn't scale.

In practice, most labs mix both, shifting toward sparser rewards as models improve.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
Whether an AI lab relies on sparse end-of-task rewards or builds human-scaffolded curricula depends primarily on base model capability, outcome verifiability, and vulnerability to reward hacking. Sparse terminal rewards only yield a learning signal if the model occasionally reaches correct solutions during exploration; when initial pass rates are near zero over long horizons, gradients vanish and labs must use staged curricula or cold-start demonstrations to bootstrap competence.

Verifiability is equally decisive. In domains like mathematics and software engineering, automated checks make binary outcome rewards cheap and tamper-resistant, allowing large-scale compute to uncover emergent reasoning strategies unconstrained by human priors—whereas human-designed intermediate rewards often invite reward hacking and cap ceiling performance. Conversely, when tasks are subjective, open-ended, or unfold in slow, stateful environments with noisy terminal signals, sparse rewards leave credit assignment intractable. In those settings, or when tighter compute budgets demand higher sample efficiency, labs invest in human-scaffolded subgoals, difficulty progression, and denser rubric-based feedback to steer exploration reliably.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
It mostly comes down to whether sparse reward gives the model any learning signal at all, and whether that is cheaper than paying humans for one.

The deciding question is whether the current policy ever succeeds. If a model solves a task even occasionally (pass@k is above zero), an end-of-task reward like "tests pass" or "answer matches" is enough. Methods like GRPO can boost the rare successes, and sparse outcome rewards scale cheaply with compute. When tasks are long, exploration is hard, or success is close to zero, the reward almost never fires. Labs then add scaffolding: expert demonstrations, graded subtasks, partial-credit rubrics, process supervision, or curricula ordered from easy to hard.

Verifiability matters as well. Math and code have cheap, reliable checkers. Fuzzier domains like law, medicine or research taste need human-written rubrics or reward models just to define success. Reward hacking also pushes toward denser supervision, because outcome-only rewards can be gamed in ways that step-level checks catch.

Then there is the bitter-lesson tradeoff. Human scaffolding costs money, doesn't scale well, and can build in human biases. Sparse rewards are general but waste compute. Labs pick the mix that gets the most capability per dollar for each domain, and they usually remove the scaffolding as models improve.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: Whether an AI lab builds human-scaffolded curricula or relies on sparse end-of-task rewards depends primarily on exploration difficulty, outcome verifiability, and the tradeoff between compute and human inductive bias. Sparse outcome rewards work best when final answers are objectively and cheaply verifiable—such as in mathematics or unit-tested code—and when the base model is already strong enough to reach correct solutions during rollouts. Under those conditions, sparse rewards scale cleanly with compute and avoid capping performance with human reasoning priors, allowing models to discover emergent strategies on their own. Conversely, when tasks involve long horizons or near-zero initial pass rates, sparse rewards produce uninformative zero-gradient trajectories; labs then use staged curricula, supervised warm-starts, or intermediate scaffolding to bridge the exploration gap and improve sample efficiency. Human-designed curricula and rubrics are also necessary in open-ended domains where final outcomes are noisy or prone to reward hacking. In practice, labs default to sparse rewards whenever compute and verifiers sustain learning, adding human scaffolding where exploration stalls or verification fails.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
The main question is whether the starting model succeeds often enough for an end-of-task reward to teach it. If the model already has the relevant skills, can discover successful approaches through trial and error, and gets a reliable score from a verifier or simulator, a lab can often use sparse rewards and spend more of its budget on rollouts.

Human scaffolding becomes more valuable when early successes are rare, tasks require many dependent steps, or the final score is hard to judge. Easier examples, demonstrations, and intermediate feedback can help the model find successful approaches and learn which decisions contributed to them. The tradeoff is the cost of building and maintaining that scaffolding versus the compute spent on unproductive attempts. Labs can also combine the two by sequencing tasks from easy to hard while still scoring only the final outcome.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
The practical test is whether the current model can succeed often enough on its own, and whether the lab can reliably recognize success. If a model sometimes solves a coding task and a test suite accurately checks the result, an end-of-task reward can reinforce successful attempts without anyone specifying how to solve it.

If nearly every attempt earns the same zero, the reward gives the model little guidance about which actions helped. A lab may then invest in demonstrations, easier precursor tasks, or verifiable milestones until the model can solve the full task often enough to learn from the outcome. A different problem arises when success itself is hard to judge. In that case, the lab may need human evaluation or a better reward signal even if the model is already capable.

The tradeoff is the cost of designing scaffolding against the compute needed to discover successes through trial and error. As the model improves, the same task may need less scaffolding.
